clinicalPearls: Characterised by polysyndactyly together with macrocephaly and a broad, high forehead
Preaxial polydactyly (often of the feet) and cutaneous syndactyly are typical, though postaxial digits also occur
Hypertelorism and frontal bossing complete the craniofacial picture
Intellect is usually normal, an important distinction from allelic and overlapping syndromes
Caused by loss-of-function GLI3 variants, including whole-gene deletions, translocations and truncating variants at the ends of the gene
Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity
Allelic with Pallister-Hall syndrome, which arises from a distinct pattern of GLI3 variant
reference.pathophysiology: Greig cephalopolysyndactyly is caused by loss-of-function variants in GLI3, including whole-gene deletions, chromosomal translocations disrupting the gene, and truncating variants near its ends, all of which reduce the amount of functional protein (haploinsufficiency). GLI3 is the key transcriptional effector of hedgehog signalling, a pathway assembled and processed on the primary cilium, so reduced GLI3 dosage disturbs the ciliary hedgehog signalling that patterns the limbs and skull. This produces the preaxial polysyndactyly, macrocephaly, frontal bossing and hypertelorism characteristic of the condition. The contrast with Pallister-Hall syndrome, caused by truncating variants in the middle of the same gene that favour a repressor form, illustrates how the position and type of GLI3 variant determine the resulting phenotype.
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the hands and feet to characterise the polysyndactyly
Chromosomal microarray to detect deletions involving GLI3
Sequencing of GLI3 when microarray is normal
Developmental assessment to document the typically preserved cognition
Brain imaging if macrocephaly is marked or neurological signs are present
redFlags: Marked macrocephaly requiring exclusion of hydrocephalus
Any developmental regression prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Complex hand or foot malformation significantly affecting function
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, with normal life expectancy and usually normal intellect; management centres on surgical correction of the limb anomalies and appropriate genetic counselling.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Pallister-Hall syndrome despite the shared GLI3 gene
Relying on sequencing alone and missing a whole-gene deletion detectable by microarray
Assuming intellectual disability, which is usually absent
Overlooking the autosomal dominant recurrence risk when counselling the family
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Surgical correction of the limb anomalies, with separation of cutaneous syndactyly and excision of duplicated preaxial or postaxial digits by paediatric hand and orthopaedic surgery
Occupational therapy and physiotherapy to optimise hand function and mobility after reconstruction
Monitor head growth and neurodevelopment given the macrocephaly, reassuring families that intellect is usually preserved
Obtain brain imaging and neurosurgical review if macrocephaly is marked or progressive or neurological signs appear, to exclude hydrocephalus or a structural anomaly
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across clinical genetics, plastic and hand surgery and paediatrics
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity, with family screening and predictive or prenatal testing for the familial GLI3 variant
